raw_segments.text: To these great examples I wish to add a lesser one. Still it bears some resemblance to them,
and I wish it to suffice me for all of a like kind. It is Hiero the Syracusean.
This man rose from a private station to be Prince of Syracuse, nor did he either owe
anything to fortune but opportunity, for the Syracuseans, being oppressed, chose him for
their captain. Afterwards he was rewarded by being made their prince.
He was of so great ability, even as a private citizen, that one who writes of him says he
wanted nothing but a kingdom to be a king. This man abolished the old soldiery, organized the
new, gave up old alliances, made new ones, and as he had his own soldiers and allies,
on such foundations he was able to build any edifice. Thus, whilst he had endured much
trouble in acquiring, he had but little in keeping.
